description: Versailles, November Criminals, Spartacist Rising — Weimar's brutal birth in 1919.
content_html:
Germany Defeated: the World War One Legacy

When the guns fell silent on 11 November 1918, Germany did not surrender on the battlefield. German troops still occupied foreign soil, and many soldiers returned home undefeated. Yet within weeks, the Kaiser had abdicated, a republic had been proclaimed, and German politicians had signed an armistice. This disconnect between military reality and political outcome would poison German democracy for the next fifteen years.

Key Fact

The Treaty of Versailles (June 1919) imposed on Germany: war guilt (Article 231), reparations of £6.6 billion (set 1921), loss of 13% of territory, the Rhineland demilitarised, and the army limited to 100,000 men.

The Treaty of Versailles, 1919

The Treaty of Versailles was signed by the new German government on 28 June 1919. German representatives were not allowed to negotiate — they were simply handed the document and told to sign. The treaty's main terms were devastating:

War guilt: Article 231, the ‘War Guilt Clause’, forced Germany to accept sole responsibility for the war. This had enormous moral and financial consequences. Reparations: Germany was required to pay compensation for war damage. The final figure, set in 1921, was £6.6 billion — a sum many economists believed impossible to pay in full. Territorial losses: Germany lost 13% of its European territory, including Alsace-Lorraine (to France), Eupen and Malmedy (to Belgium), North Schleswig (to Denmark after a plebiscite), Posen and West Prussia (to the newly created Poland). Danzig became a free city under League of Nations supervision. German colonies were redistributed as ‘mandates’ among the Allies. Military restrictions: The German army was limited to 100,000 men, no tanks or aircraft, and the navy was stripped of its main fleet. The Rhineland was demilitarised.

Germans across the political spectrum condemned the treaty as a Diktat — a peace dictated by force rather than agreed by negotiation. Many had expected a settlement based on Woodrow Wilson’s Fourteen Points, which promised national self-determination and no punitive terms. Instead they received humiliation. The army was outraged by the military clauses; industrialists feared reparations would cripple the economy; nationalists raged at territorial losses that left millions of German-speakers under foreign rule.

The politicians who signed the armistice in November 1918 were branded November Criminals by right-wing groups who claimed they had ‘stabbed Germany in the back’ by surrendering when the army could still have fought on. This ‘stab-in-the-back myth’ was historically false — the German High Command had itself requested an armistice because the military situation was hopeless — but it was politically powerful and would fuel right-wing resentment throughout the Weimar period.

The Birth of the Weimar Republic

On 9 November 1918, Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated and Friedrich Ebert of the Social Democrat Party (SPD) became head of government. Two days later, the armistice was signed. In February 1919, a new constitution was drawn up at Weimar, giving the republic its name. The Weimar Constitution created a democratic system with proportional representation, where seats in the Reichstag were allocated in direct proportion to votes cast. This ensured that even small parties gained representation, but it also meant coalition governments were the norm and decisive majorities were rare.

Key Fact

Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution allowed the President to rule by emergency decree, bypassing the Reichstag. It was designed for genuine crises, but was used 136 times between 1930 and 1932, undermining parliamentary democracy.

Political Instability: the Spartacist Rising, 1919

The new republic faced violent opposition from both left and right from its first weeks. In January 1919, the Spartacists, led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, launched an armed uprising in Berlin. Inspired by the Bolshevik revolution in Russia, they seized newspaper offices and called on workers to overthrow the government. Ebert called in the Freikorps — right-wing volunteer ex-soldiers — to crush the revolt. The Freikorps suppressed the rising brutally; both Luxemburg and Liebknecht were murdered in custody in January 1919. The use of the Freikorps to defend the republic permanently alienated the German left from Ebert’s government.

Right-wing opposition erupted in March 1920 when the Kapp Putsch attempted to seize power in Berlin. Wolfgang Kapp, a nationalist politician, and General Walther von Lüttwitz marched Freikorps units into Berlin and declared a new government. The regular army refused to fire on the Freikorps. The Weimar government fled the capital. The putsch collapsed within four days when Berlin’s trade unions called a general strike that paralysed the city — transport, power and water all stopped. Kapp fled to Sweden. The episode revealed the fragility of the new republic: it had been saved not by its own security forces but by workers' industrial action.

The weakness of both putsches showed the deep divisions in German society. Left-wing workers, nationalist ex-soldiers, conservative businessmen and rural landowners had completely incompatible visions of Germany’s future. The Weimar Republic sat at the centre of these conflicts, lacking the broad popular legitimacy needed to command loyalty in a crisis.

Structural Weaknesses of the Weimar System

Beyond immediate crises, the republic had deeper structural problems. Proportional representation produced weak coalition governments that frequently collapsed. Between 1919 and 1933, Germany had twenty different cabinets. Article 48 gave the President emergency powers that could bypass parliament entirely. The judiciary and civil service were largely staffed by men loyal to the old imperial order, and treated the republic’s enemies with leniency: Hitler received a light sentence for his 1923 coup attempt, while left-wing defendants faced far harsher treatment. The army remained a ‘state within the state’, never fully committed to democratic government.
exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark ‘Explain the significance’ question on the Treaty of Versailles, you need to address significance at the time AND over time. At the time: it caused immediate political instability and financial hardship. Over time: it fuelled resentment that Hitler exploited in the 1930s. Avoid simply listing the treaty’s terms — the question tests analysis, not description. For a 6-mark ‘Explain a cause’ question on Weimar instability, pick one cause (such as proportional representation) and develop it with specific detail and a link to consequence.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Treaty of Versailles (1919) imposed war guilt, £6.6 billion reparations, 13% territorial losses and military restrictions that outraged German opinion across the political spectrum.
  • The ‘stab-in-the-back myth’ falsely blamed democratic politicians (the ‘November Criminals’) for Germany’s defeat, poisoning Weimar democracy from birth.
  • The Spartacist Rising (1919) and Kapp Putsch (1920) showed violent opposition from both left and right; structural weaknesses — proportional representation, Article 48, a hostile judiciary — made stable government extremely difficult.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Treaty of Versailles that affected Germany's military strength.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific military clause (e.g. army limited to 100,000 men) AND adds precise detail (no tanks, no aircraft, navy stripped). Secure: identifies a military clause with some supporting detail. Developing: names a clause without detail. Emerging: vague reference to military restrictions.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Weimar Constitution that made it difficult to govern Germany.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4): two features each developed with precise detail — e.g. proportional representation led to coalition governments that were frequently unstable (20 cabinets 1919–1933); Article 48 allowed presidential rule by emergency decree, used 136 times 1930–1932, undermining parliament. Secure (3): two features with some development. Developing (2): two features briefly identified. Emerging (1): one feature identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Spartacist Rising of January 1919.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): identifies a clear cause (e.g. revolutionary socialism inspired by the Bolshevik revolution of 1917; workers' suffering under wartime conditions; anger at the new SPD government's moderate policies) AND develops it with specific supporting detail AND shows how it led directly to the uprising. Secure (3–4): clear cause with development but limited linkage to consequence. Developing (2): cause identified with brief explanation. Emerging (1): simple, undeveloped point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Kapp Putsch for the Weimar Republic.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): identifies a precise consequence (e.g. the putsch revealed the army's disloyalty — it refused to fire on the Freikorps; the republic was saved by trade-union general strike, not its own forces; this exposed the weakness of Weimar's security apparatus) AND develops the consequence with specific evidence AND shows further effects. Secure (3–4): consequence identified and developed. Developing (2): consequence identified with limited explanation. Emerging (1): vague mention of consequences.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 'stab-in-the-back' myth for the development of German politics in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): addresses significance at the time (immediate political impact — delegitimising the republic, fuelling right-wing violence, targeting democratic politicians) AND over time (Hitler's use of the myth to justify overthrowing Weimar in the 1930s) with specific evidence throughout. Secure (5–6): significance addressed with development; may focus more on one time period. Developing (3–4): some analysis of significance but limited to description or one time period. Emerging (1–2): simple points about the myth without analytical development.

practice_questions.text: 'The Treaty of Versailles was the main reason why the Weimar Republic faced serious problems in its early years.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): sustained argument agreeing AND disagreeing — agrees: Versailles created economic hardship, war-guilt resentment, stab-in-the-back myth, right-wing anger; disagrees: structural weaknesses (proportional representation, Article 48), political extremism (Spartacists, Freikorps), economic disruption pre-dated Versailles. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7–9): both perspectives developed with evidence; judgement present. Developing (4–6): one side developed more than the other; limited overall judgement. Emerging (1–3): descriptive with little analytical engagement.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the total reparations figure set for Germany in 1921?
Which of the following groups crushed the Spartacist Rising in January 1919?
The Article of the Treaty of Versailles that forced Germany to accept sole responsibility for the war was Article _____.
The _____ Putsch of March 1920 attempted to overthrow the Weimar Republic but collapsed when Berlin's trade unions called a general strike.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: German politicians falsely blamed for betraying an undefeated army
Emergency powers allowing the President to bypass the Reichstag
A peace settlement imposed by force without negotiation

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Treaty of Versailles signed?
What did Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles require Germany to accept?
flashcard_questions.a: Sole responsibility (war guilt) for the First World War.

flashcard_questions.q: What reparations figure was set for Germany in 1921?
What percentage of Germany's European territory was lost under Versailles?
What German term described the Treaty of Versailles as a dictated peace?
Who was the first President of the Weimar Republic?

flashcard_questions.a: The false claim that democratic politicians betrayed an undefeated German army in 1918.

flashcard_questions.q: Who led the Spartacist Rising in January 1919?
What happened to Luxemburg and Liebknecht after the Spartacist Rising?
flashcard_questions.a: They were murdered by Freikorps soldiers in January 1919.

flashcard_questions.q: Who launched the Kapp Putsch in March 1920?
flashcard_questions.a: Wolfgang Kapp, backed by Freikorps units under General von Lüttwitz.

flashcard_questions.q: How was the Kapp Putsch defeated?
flashcard_questions.a: Berlin's trade unions called a general strike that paralysed the city within four days.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution allow the President to do?
flashcard_questions.a: Rule by emergency decree, bypassing the Reichstag.

flashcard_questions.q: How many different cabinets did Germany have between 1919 and 1933?

glossary_terms.definition: The peace settlement signed in June 1919 that formally ended the First World War and imposed harsh terms on Germany.
The German term meaning 'dictated peace', used to describe the Treaty of Versailles, which Germany was forced to sign without negotiation.
The accusation levelled at German democratic politicians who signed the 1918 armistice, falsely claiming they betrayed an undefeated army.
The first President of the Weimar Republic (1919–1925), a Social Democrat who oversaw the republic's difficult birth.
A far-left revolutionary group that staged an uprising in Berlin in January 1919, aiming to create a Soviet-style communist state in Germany.
A right-wing attempt to overthrow the Weimar Republic in March 1920, led by Wolfgang Kapp and supported by the Freikorps.
